response.title: how to power a well pump when the power is out
response.answer:
If your home uses a private well pump, you can keep water running during a power outage using a portable generator, battery backup, or solar-powered system.

The best solution depends on whether your well pump runs on 120V or 240V, its horsepower, and how long you need backup water.

1. Four ways to power a well pump during an outage
Shop

Option 1: Portable generator

Best for most homes

A 240V generator can power many residential well pumps. A typical setup costs roughly $600–$2,000 for the generator, plus electrical installation.

Requires a properly installed transfer switch or interlock.

Shop

Option 2: Battery power station

Quiet, no gasoline, and potentially usable indoors. However, many power stations only provide 120V, while well pumps commonly require 240V.

Look for 240V output and sufficient motor-starting capacity.

Shop

Option 3: Solar panels + battery

Good for extended outages. You need a hybrid inverter capable of operating without grid power and starting the well pump.

Solar panels alone generally won't work during an outage.

Shop

Option 4: Automatic standby generator

Automatically starts during outages and can power the well pump along with other household circuits.

More expensive, but convenient for frequent outages.

2. How much power does a well pump need?

Most residential submersible well pumps use 240V. Their starting power can be several times their normal running power.

Pump size

5,000–9,000 W

These are planning estimates. Actual requirements depend on the pump motor, depth, wiring, and starting system. Use the pump manufacturer's electrical specifications to size the backup source.

3. How do you connect a generator to the pump?
Conceptual connection: a transfer switch safely selects grid or generator power for the well pump circuit.

Important safety considerations:

Never connect a generator directly to a household outlet or breaker panel without approved transfer equipment.

Never run a fuel-powered generator indoors, in a garage, or near windows or vents.

Have a licensed electrician install the transfer equipment and verify voltage, grounding, and motor-starting capacity.
